passage:
My cousin Hrithik called on Thursday. His catering stall needed someone to run it for a month, and he wanted me to drop my internship for it. When I said I couldn't, he said, "You only think of yourself." That stung, more than I expected. I felt my face go hot, and I wanted to shout back or give in just to end the call.
Instead I took a breath. "I can't leave the internship. It is what I have worked for. But I can come two evenings a week, and I'll ask a friend from my class if she wants some part-time work." He was quiet, then said, "Two evenings is something."
He didn't say thank you that day. But on Sunday he sent me the stall's schedule.
Joseph

qa.q: On which day did Hrithik call?
qa.a: Hrithik called on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling after being told 'You only think of yourself'?
qa.a: Joseph felt stung and hot in the face, tempted to shout back or give in just to end the call.

qa.q: What could Joseph do or did do that was fairer than yielding or fighting?
qa.a: Joseph calmly explained that the internship could not be dropped, and offered two evenings a week and a friend's part-time help.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt when Joseph said no to running the stall?
qa.a: Hrithik was probably disappointed and worried about the stall, which is why he snapped, but he was quiet and then said that two evenings is something.

grounding: A young adult declines a family demand and hears they only think of themselves, then explains limits calmly and offers help elsewhere.

passage:
Mentor note, written by Amandeep.
Pradeep, a final-year student, told me on Wednesday that an uncle had asked him to come home for the whole week of a family wedding and skip his lab project deadline. When he said he could not, the uncle told him he only thought of himself. Pradeep said the words stayed with him all night, and he admitted he was tempted to say yes just to make it stop.
I did not tell him what to do. We talked about which parts he could offer. On Friday he phoned his uncle and calmly said he could not miss the deadline, but he would come on Saturday and help with the guest list. The uncle went quiet, then agreed. Pradeep looked lighter when he told me.

qa.q: What did the uncle ask Pradeep to do for the wedding?
qa.a: The uncle asked him to come home for the whole week of the family wedding and skip his lab project deadline.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling after being told he only thought of himself?
qa.a: Pradeep felt hurt and pressured, since the words stayed with him all night and he was tempted to say yes just to make it stop.

qa.q: What did Pradeep choose to do on Friday, and why was it a fair way to answer?
qa.a: He calmly told his uncle he could not miss the deadline but offered to come on Saturday and help with the guest list, which set a limit and still gave support.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have seen Pradeep's call to the uncle?
qa.a: Amandeep seems to have seen it as a good step, noting that Pradeep looked lighter afterwards, and had left the choice to Pradeep by not telling him what to do.

grounding: A young adult who declines a family demand is called selfish, and calmly explaining limits and offering help elsewhere is fairer.

passage:
In the college hostel office in Ranchi, the phone rang for Vinita, twenty. It was her uncle. "Your cousin's wedding is next week. We need you home for ten days to help with everything."
"Chachaji, my semester exams start on Monday. I can come for the last two days."
"Two days! Everyone else is making time. You only think of yourself."
Vinita's throat tightened. She could hear her cousin Sahil in the background: "She always does this."
She took a breath. "I'm not refusing the wedding. I'm refusing to miss my exams. I can do all the invitation designs online this week, and I'll book my ticket for the last two days."
Silence.
"Fine," her uncle said coldly, and hung up.
Vinita sat on the office bench, shaking. The warden, overhearing, said, "You were calm and fair. That's not selfish." Vinita emailed the first design that night.

qa.q: How many days did Vinita's uncle want her home?
qa.a: He wanted her home for ten days.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when her throat tightened?
qa.a: Vinita felt hurt and stung by being called selfish, and anxious about the family's anger.

qa.q: What made Vinita's response fairer than either yielding or fighting?
qa.a: She calmly explained her limit, the exams, and offered other help, the invitation designs and two days at the wedding.

qa.q: How might Sahil see Vinita's refusal?
qa.a: Sahil seems to see it as a pattern of her putting herself first, without seeing the exams she was protecting.

grounding: A young adult who declines a family demand is called selfish, and calmly explains her limits while offering help in another way.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,
You're my brother, so I'll be honest. The family group chat has gone quiet on me since I said no, and Mama told Chachi I'm "only thinking of my own future."
Here's what happened. Nani needs full-time care, and everyone decided I should drop my final year and stay home, since I'm "the girl" and "only studying." I said no. Not because I don't love Nani. I do. But I have six months left, and a scholarship I can't defer.
I've offered what I can: every weekend at home, the evening video calls with her, and I'll help find and pay part of a day nurse from my stipend.
It still stings to be called selfish. I cried on the bus yesterday.
Can you talk to Mama with me? I don't want to fight. I just want them to see I'm not abandoning anyone.
Arohi

qa.q: How many months does Arohi have left?
qa.a: She has six months left.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel about being called selfish?
qa.a: Arohi feels stung and hurt, crying on the bus, even though she loves Nani.

qa.q: What makes Arohi's response fair?
qa.a: She calmly explains her limit, finishing her final year, and offers help in other ways, weekends at home, calls with Nani and help finding a day nurse.

qa.q: How might Nani feel if she knew about the argument?
qa.a: Nani might feel sad to be the cause of tension, and perhaps glad Arohi is finishing her studies.

grounding: A young adult who declines to give up her studies for a family demand is called selfish, and calmly explains her limits while offering other help.

passage:
Lalremsiami, you asked why I don't drive my cousins everywhere anymore. Here's the story.
After I got my licence, I became the family's free driver. Weddings, airports, grocery runs, at midnight, at six a.m. I said yes to everything. Then I got an internship at a design studio, and I had to be there by nine every day.
My uncle wanted me to drive my cousin to her coaching every morning at eight-thirty. I said, "I can't, Chachu, I'll be late for work. I can drive on Sundays." He said, "Jasleen has become selfish since she got that internship."
It hurt, honestly. I lay awake thinking maybe he was right.
But I kept calm. I told my cousin I'd teach her the bus route, and I did, on a Sunday. I still drive on Sundays.
Some of them still call me selfish. I've accepted that. I'm Jasleen, and saying no kindly is not a crime.

qa.q: What time did Jasleen have to be at the design studio?
qa.a: She had to be there by nine every day.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when her uncle called her selfish?
qa.a: Jasleen felt hurt and doubtful, lying awake wondering if he was right.

qa.q: What made Jasleen's approach fair?
qa.a: She calmly explained her limit, offered to drive on Sundays, and taught her cousin the bus route instead of simply refusing or fighting.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's cousin feel after learning the bus route?
qa.a: The cousin may feel more independent and grateful, even if she first missed the rides.

grounding: A young adult who says no to a family demand is called selfish, and calmly explains her limits while offering help in other ways.

passage:
Monday. Bua called: Yamini must come to Jaipur for the whole wedding week and manage the caterers. Her CA exam was eight days after the wedding. "I can't take the whole week, Bua," Yamini said. Bua's voice went cold. "Always thinking of yourself. We raised you like our own." Yamini put the phone down and cried in the stairwell.
Wednesday. Her cousin Tushar, the groom, messaged: "Mummy's upset. Just come, yaar." Yamini typed three angry replies and deleted them. Then she called him. "I love you both. I can't lose this exam. But I can do the whole guest list and the caterer calls from here, tonight and tomorrow."
Saturday. Tushar sent a photo of the finished guest list pinned up in Bua's kitchen. "Mummy says your list is neater than hers." Bua still hasn't called. But she forwarded the mehendi photos to Yamini first.

qa.q: When was Yamini's CA exam?
qa.a: It was eight days after the wedding.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling after Bua called her selfish?
qa.a: Yamini was deeply hurt, crying in the stairwell because the label stung coming from someone who raised her.

qa.q: Why did Yamini's call to Tushar work better than her angry replies would have?
qa.a: She calmly explained her limit, said she loved them and offered concrete help from home, avoiding both giving in and fighting.

qa.q: How might Bua be feeling by Saturday?
qa.a: Bua seems still a little hurt but softening; not calling yet sending the mehendi photos to Yamini first hints at quiet reconciliation.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult called selfish for declining a family demand, who calmly explains limits and offers help elsewhere instead of yielding or fighting.
